lessons.title: Why Designing With AI Is Different

items: State the two root causes of AI design difficulty
Explain why Wizard-of-Oz misleads for LLMs
Adopt the probabilistic-product mindset

reading.text: Part X is about building things, and it opens by naming why the ordinary design process fails here. The claim is not that AI products are harder in the way that complex products are harder — it is that two specific properties break tools designers rely on.
The design-material problem

Yang, Steinfeld, Rosé & Zimmerman, "Re-examining Whether, Why, and How Human-AI Interaction Is Uniquely Difficult to Design" (CHI 2020): two root causes — capability uncertainty and output open-endedness.

Capability uncertainty means you cannot know in advance what the system will be able to do, so you cannot scope the design against a specification. Output open-endedness means you cannot enumerate what it will produce, so you cannot design every state it might land in. Together they break sketching, which assumes you can represent the thing before building it.

The practical conclusion is that prototyping has to include the real model. Designing on paper produces a design for an imagined system, and the imagined system is always more consistent than the real one.

Wizard-of-Oz systematically misleads for LLMs: a human confederate produces sensible, consistent, competent responses — precisely the behaviours the real system will fail to deliver, and precisely the ones the design must handle.

This is worth stating strongly because Wizard-of-Oz is a trusted technique elsewhere, and here it inverts. It tests an experience the product cannot provide, and it skips every failure mode — confident wrongness, inconsistency between runs, misread intent — that actually determines whether the product is usable.

Leaky abstractions (Subramonyam et al., CHI 2024): prompt-based development leaks model internals into UX decisions, the design and engineering handoff dissolves, and designers must play with the material — actual model behaviour — directly.

The dissolved handoff is a real organisational consequence, not just a methodological note. If the phrasing of a prompt changes the product's behaviour, then writing that phrasing is a design act performed in a place designers traditionally do not go — and a process that keeps them out of it has put the design decisions in the wrong hands.
The probabilistic-product mindset
Define an acceptable-failure envelope per feature, and design the 5% failure path with the same care as the 95% path. Error UX is the product.

In a deterministic product, failure is exceptional and its handling can be proportionate to its rarity. In a probabilistic one, failure is a normal operating state occurring at a known rate — so designing only the success path leaves a large fraction of the actual experience undesigned.

The failure envelope is the discipline that makes this tractable: for each feature, state what kinds of wrong are tolerable and at what rate. That number then determines how much oversight, recovery and containment the design owes — which turns an unbounded worry into a specification.

Subramonyam et al., leaky abstractions (CHI 2024)

cards.front: The two root causes of AI design difficulty
cards.back: Capability uncertainty — you don't know what it can do — and output open-endedness — you can't enumerate what it will produce (Yang et al. 2020).

cards.front: Why does Wizard-of-Oz mislead for LLMs?
cards.back: The human confederate is competent and consistent, so the prototype tests an experience the real system will not deliver, and skips the failure modes that matter.
Model internals leak into UX decisions, so the clean design/engineering handoff dissolves and designers must work with model behaviour directly.
A per-feature specification of what kinds and rates of failure are tolerable — which then determines how much oversight and recovery the design must supply.

quiz.question: A team prototypes an AI feature with a human pretending to be the model. What will they systematically miss?
options: The failure modes — confident wrongness, inconsistency, misread intent — that define the real experience
quiz.why: A competent human confederate produces the behaviour the model won't. The 5% path is where the design work lives, and Wizard-of-Oz hides it.

quiz.question: What does "error UX is the product" mean in practice?
options: The failure path deserves the same design investment as the success path, because it is a routine rather than exceptional state
quiz.why: In a probabilistic product, failure is a normal operating state at a known rate. Designing only the happy path leaves most of the experience undesigned.

items: Apply a working pattern language for AI products
Name and avoid the anti-patterns

reading.text: This chapter is the practical distillation of everything before it. Read each pattern with its justification attached — almost all of them are gulf-bridging devices, and knowing which gulf a pattern addresses tells you when it will not help.
The pattern language

items: Draft-then-refine — the AI proposes, the human disposes. Preserves authorship and keeps the artefact inspectable.
Inline generation with diff — reduces verification cost by making checking proportional to the change rather than the document.
Suggestion chips and capability scent — restores information scent to an interface that emits none (Ch. 9).
Progressive autonomy — widen the approval envelope as reliability is demonstrated; a levels-of-automation slider made legible (Ch. 28).
Plan preview, step approval, rollback — agent oversight with an intervention point before commitment.
Grounded answers with inspectable citations — manufactures evaluability where fluency removed it (Ch. 33).
Confidence-scaled friction — act silently when cheap to reverse, confirm when not. Horvitz operationalised.
Memory transparency panel — view, edit, delete; contextual integrity made operable (Ch. 30).
Expectation-setting onboarding — show what it is bad at early (Kocielnik, Ch. 29).
Repair-friendly history — edit any turn, branch, compare; conversation as a manipulable object (Ch. 32).

reading.text: Two of those carry more weight than the rest. Draft-then-refine is the shape most AI features should take, because it puts generation where delegation pays and correction where the human is needed. And confidence-scaled friction is the one that prevents the two opposite failures — an assistant that interrupts constantly, and one that acts irreversibly without asking.
Anti-patterns

items: Fake typing theatre — artificial delay presented as work
Unlabelled AI content
Sycophantic tone defaults
Approval fatigue from over-confirmation
"AI sparkle" buttons with no scent of function

reading.text: Approval fatigue is the one that masquerades as diligence. Confirming everything looks careful and trains dismissal, so the confirmation that guards something irreversible gets clicked through with all the others — the cry-wolf effect from chapter 20, arriving through good intentions.

The sparkle button is the purest signifier failure in the set: an icon that announces AI is involved while saying nothing about what will happen. It marks a technology rather than an action, which is not what a label is for.
Almost every pattern here is a gulf-bridging device. Chips and scaffolds narrow execution; diffs, citations and plan previews narrow evaluation. The pattern language is chapter 6 applied.

Industry references worth studying as compiled research rather than as style guides: the Microsoft HAX Toolkit, the Google PAIR Guidebook, Apple's HIG machine-learning sections, and IBM Carbon for AI.

items: Microsoft HAX Toolkit
Google PAIR Guidebook
Apple Human Interface Guidelines, machine learning and generative sections
IBM Carbon for AI

cards.back: The AI proposes and the human disposes. It preserves authorship and keeps the artefact inspectable and editable.
Widen the agent's approval envelope as it demonstrates reliability — a levels-of-automation slider made legible to the user.
Act silently when the action is cheap to reverse; confirm when it is not. Horvitz's expected-utility rule, operationalised.

cards.front: Why is approval fatigue an anti-pattern?
cards.back: Undifferentiated confirmation trains dismissal, so the confirmation that matters gets clicked through with the rest — the cry-wolf effect.
A button marked as AI-powered that gives no indication of what it will do — an icon standing in for a signifier.
Treat the conversation as a manipulable object: edit any turn, branch from it, and compare results.

quiz.question: Which pattern most directly attacks verification cost?
quiz.why: A diff shows exactly what changed, so checking scales with the size of the change rather than the size of the document.

quiz.question: A product confirms every agent action, including trivially reversible ones. Which anti-pattern is this?
quiz.why: Confirming everything makes confirmation meaningless. Friction has to be proportionate to stakes and reversibility or it stops carrying signal.

quiz.question: Suggestion chips solve which problem, in the book's terms?
options: Absent information scent in an interface that signals no capabilities
quiz.why: A blank input emits no cue about what will pay off. Chips restore scent and simultaneously act as signifiers for invisible affordances.

items: Design the four stages of AI error recovery
Communicate confidence without raw percentages
Onboard by guided doing

reading.text: If failure is a normal operating state, then the failure path is a designed surface rather than an exception handler. This chapter is about what that surface contains.
Four stages

AI error recovery has four stages: detect — make errors detectable through contrast and grounding; attribute — explain why it failed in the user's terms; repair — a one-step correction that also teaches the system; and contain — blast-radius limits through sandboxes, drafts and undo.

They are sequential and each is a separate design problem. Detection is the hardest and the most neglected, because fluent wrong output supplies no cue at all — everything else in the sequence is unreachable if the user never notices. Attribution turns a failure into something the user can reason about rather than a mystery that erodes trust generally. Repair should cost one action, not a restart. Containment accepts that some failures will get through and bounds what they can do.
Undo is the single highest-leverage trust feature in agentic products. It converts a decision about whether to trust into a decision that can be revisited.

That is worth understanding mechanically. Without undo, every delegation is a bet, and the rational response to a bet you cannot unwind is to supervise it closely — which removes the benefit of delegating. With undo, the cost of being wrong drops, and the user can afford to let the system act.
Confidence

Confidence visualisation: avoid raw percentages, which are both miscalibrated and misread. Prefer behaviour-linked confidence — "I checked three sources", "I could not verify X" — selective abstention, and uncertainty-adaptive phrasing. Where numbers are needed, use chapter 18's uncertainty toolkit.

A verbalised percentage fails twice over. The number itself is poorly calibrated, so it does not mean what it claims; and a precise-looking figure is read as authoritative, so it is over-trusted in exactly the way chapter 29 warns about. Behaviour-linked statements avoid both because they describe something checkable — a claim about what the system did, which the user can verify.
Onboarding

Onboarding to AI: teach the envelope by guided doing — first-run tasks that hit both a strength and a graceful failure. Expectation calibration beats capability advertising (Kocielnik et al. 2019), and advanced prompting should arrive by progressive disclosure.

The counterintuitive move is deliberately showing a new user something the system is bad at, early, while the stakes are zero. A first run composed only of impressive successes sets a boundary the system cannot hold, so the first real failure lands as a betrayal rather than a known limitation.

Users who learn the failure boundary from a safe demonstration calibrate faster than users who discover it in production — which is the same argument chapter 29 makes about knowing when a system errs, moved to the first five minutes.

items: Kocielnik et al., Will You Accept an Imperfect AI? (CHI 2019)
the uncertainty visualisation work from chapter 18
Hullman, Kay et al.

cards.front: The four stages of AI error recovery
The highest-leverage trust feature in agentic products
cards.back: Undo. It turns an irreversible bet on trust into a revisable decision.
Expressing certainty through what the system did — sources checked, claims it could not verify — rather than a numeric score users misread.

cards.front: Why show a new user a failure on purpose?
cards.back: Expectation calibration beats capability advertising. A safe early failure teaches the envelope faster than discovering it in production.
The maximum damage an erroneous action can do. Sandboxes, drafts and staged execution shrink it before trust is established.

quiz.question: Why avoid displaying "87% confident" on an LLM answer?
options: Verbalised LLM confidence is miscalibrated, and users misread percentages as precision
quiz.why: The number is both wrong and read as authoritative. Behaviour-linked statements say something checkable instead.

quiz.question: An onboarding flow demonstrates only impressive successes. What does the evidence predict?
options: Poorly calibrated expectations, so the first real failure lands harder and reliance is miscalibrated in both directions
quiz.why: Kocielnik et al. found expectation setting shifts acceptance. Advertising only strengths sets a boundary the system cannot hold.

quiz.question: Which recovery stage does a sandbox serve?
quiz.why: A sandbox limits the blast radius. It does nothing to make the error visible, explain it, or fix it.

lessons.title: Capstone — Design an AI-Native Product End-to-End

items: Integrate the whole book into one designed artefact
Defend every decision with a citation

reading.text: This is the course exam, and its structure is the argument: a defensible AI product requires field research, material exploration, a pattern-mapped concept, an oversight specification, a reliance-aware evaluation and an ethics audit. Skipping any one of them produces a familiar kind of failure, and each maps to a part of this book.
Seven deliverables

items: Problem framing with contextual inquiry — minimum five sessions (Ch. 14)
Model-behaviour exploration notebook — the material study (Ch. 37)
Pattern-mapped concept with an explicit gulf analysis (Ch. 38, Ch. 6)
Oversight and failure-envelope specification (Ch. 28, 35, 39)
Reliance-aware evaluation plan, piloted with eight users (Ch. 29, 36)
Ethics audit — dark-pattern scan, anthropomorphism dose, memory consent (Ch. 21, 30, 34)
Public critique presentation defending every decision with a citation from this book

reading.text: The five-session minimum on the first deliverable is the one that cannot be faked. Observed real work produces breakdowns nobody invents at a desk, and a concept built without them will be a solution to an imagined problem however well the remaining six are executed.
The cross-cutting checklists

Universal design review, applicable to any interface: where are the two gulfs widest? One preattentive singleton at most? Recognition over recall everywhere? Every action reversible, or confirmed in proportion to its cost? State changes visible where the eyes already are? Keyboard and screen-reader pass completed? Scent audit on every navigation label?

AI feature review, applicable to anything with a model behind it: is expectation-setting present before first use? Is the failure envelope specified and designed? Is a reliance metric defined — not acceptance rate? Is friction scaled to stakes multiplied by reversibility? Is there undo for every agent action? Is memory legible and editable? Is the anthropomorphism dose justified? Has sycophancy been audited? Does it pass the endorsement test?

Those two lists are the book compressed to a page. If you retain nothing else, retaining the questions is enough to catch most of what goes wrong — because each one is a finding from a chapter, phrased as something you can check.
Recommended study order for a designer targeting AI-era employment: 6 → 7 → 12 → 29 → 33 → 38 → 39 → 14 → 36 → capstone.

cards.back: Contextual-inquiry framing, model-behaviour notebook, pattern-mapped concept with gulf analysis, oversight and failure-envelope spec, reliance-aware evaluation, ethics audit, defended public critique.

cards.front: The universal design review, in one line
cards.back: Find where the two gulfs are widest, then check pop-out budget, recall load, reversibility, state visibility, accessibility and scent.

cards.front: The nine questions of the AI feature review
cards.back: Expectations set? Failure envelope designed? Reliance metric defined? Friction scaled to stakes × reversibility? Undo everywhere? Memory legible? Anthropomorphism dose justified? Sycophancy audited? Endorsement test passed?

cards.front: The recommended fast path through the book

quiz.question: Which capstone deliverable would be impossible to fake without having done the fieldwork?
quiz.why: Five sessions of observed real work produce breakdowns you cannot invent from a desk — which is why the book sets a session minimum.

quiz.question: The AI feature review asks for a reliance metric "not acceptance rate." Why?
options: Because acceptance cannot separate trusting correct output from trusting wrong output
Because acceptance is a business metric
Because it varies too much between users
quiz.why: Appropriate reliance requires discrimination — accept-when-right minus accept-when-wrong. Raw acceptance rewards indiscriminate trust.
